name: James Keller
bio: James Keller was a foreign-born resident ordered deported for political reasons but whom no country would accept, leaving him under lifetime 'supervisory parole' under the McCarran-Walter Act. He was arrested and indicted in Chicago in late 1955 — one of the first such test prosecutions — for refusing, on First and Fifth Amendment grounds, to answer his parole officers' questions about his associates.
charges: McCarran-Walter Act — violating supervisory parole by refusing to answer questions
sentence: Faced a year in jail and a $1,000 fine

name: Polychronis Paschalidis
bio: Polychronis 'Paul' Paschalidis was the New York secretary of the Federation of Greek Maritime Unions, outlawed in Greece, held in U.S. immigration detention and ordered deported to Greece, where he faced imprisonment or death. After being brought within minutes of being put on a plane in June 1956, his attorney won a court stay, and he was allowed to depart instead for asylum in Poland in August 1956.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran-Walter Act — to Greece
convicted: Detained for deportation; won a stay; departed for Poland 1956
sentence: Deportation detention; voluntary departure to Poland

name: Frank Borich
bio: Frank Borich was the Croatian-born head of the National Miners Union during the 1931 coal strikes, repeatedly arrested and detained for deportation over two decades for his radical labor organizing. Held at Ellis Island for a month in 1950 and four months in 1952 and ordered deported to Yugoslavia (which refused him), he was released to lifetime supervisory parole.
charges: Deportation under the immigration / McCarran Internal Security Act — for radical labor activity
convicted: Repeatedly detained; ordered deported; on supervisory parole
sentence: Months of detention; lifetime supervisory parole

name: William Heikkila
bio: William Heikkila was a San Francisco draftsman brought to the United States from Finland as a two-year-old infant, ordered deported under the McCarran-Walter Act over alleged past Communist association and called before the House Un-American Activities Committee in 1956. His case (Heikkila v. Barber) tested the deportation of a lifelong U.S. resident to a country he had never known.
charges: Deportation under the McCarran-Walter Act — to Finland
convicted: Ordered deported; case in the courts

name: Benjamin Saltzman
bio: Benjamin Saltzman was a foreign-born resident arrested for deportation under the McCarran-Walter Act in the Cold War crackdown on the foreign-born; his wife, a Gold Star mother, testified on his behalf before the Subversive Activities Control Board. He was defended by the American Committee for Protection of Foreign Born.

name: Martin Luther King
bio: The Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. was the 27-year-old president of the Montgomery Improvement Association when he was arrested and indicted under a 1921 Alabama anti-boycott statute for leading the Montgomery bus boycott against segregation. Tried in March 1956 — the test case for nearly 90 indicted boycotters — he was convicted and fined $500 while his home was bombed and the protest continued.
charges: Alabama anti-boycott law — for leading the Montgomery bus boycott

name: Rosa Parks
bio: Rosa Parks was the Montgomery seamstress and NAACP secretary whose arrest on December 1, 1955 for refusing to give up her bus seat to a white man sparked the Montgomery bus boycott. Convicted and fined under the segregation ordinance, she was then re-arrested in the February 1956 roundup of boycott leaders indicted under the state anti-boycott law.
charges: Bus-segregation ordinance; then the Alabama anti-boycott law
sentence: Fined $14; appeal pending; re-indicted in the boycott case

name: Ralph Abernathy
bio: The Rev. Ralph D. Abernathy was the vice-president of the Montgomery Improvement Association, indicted in 1956 under the Alabama anti-boycott law as one of the leaders of the Montgomery bus boycott. He was arrested, fingerprinted, and released on bond among the roughly 90 indicted.
charges: Alabama anti-boycott law — for leading the Montgomery bus boycott
sentence: Awaiting trial on the boycott charge

name: E. D. Nixon
bio: E. D. Nixon was a Pullman porter, longtime NAACP and union leader, and a key organizer of the Montgomery bus boycott, indicted in 1956 under the Alabama anti-boycott law. His home, like Dr. King's, was bombed during the protest.
charges: Alabama anti-boycott law — for leading the Montgomery bus boycott
sentence: Awaiting trial on the boycott charge

name: Fred D. Gray
bio: Fred D. Gray was one of only two Black lawyers in Montgomery and the attorney for the bus boycotters, Rosa Parks, and the NAACP. In 1956 he was indicted on a charge of representing a client 'without authority' (later dropped) and his draft board punitively reclassified him 1-A and ordered him to report for induction — moves widely condemned as retaliation for his civil-rights work.
charges: State indictment (representing a client without authority); punitive draft reclassification
convicted: Indicted (charge dropped); ordered to report for induction (delayed)
sentence: Charge dropped; induction delayed after protest

name: Matthew Kennedy
bio: Matthew Kennedy was a pensioned World War I veteran, over seventy, who drove in the Montgomery Improvement Association car pool and was one of the roughly 90 Black citizens of Montgomery indicted under the Alabama anti-boycott law in 1956. He said he was 'proud to be one of the 90.'
charges: Alabama anti-boycott law — for participating in the Montgomery bus boycott
sentence: Awaiting trial on the boycott charge

name: C. K. Steele
bio: The Rev. C. K. Steele was the Tallahassee NAACP president and leader of the Inter-Civic Council, which ran the Tallahassee bus boycott. In 1956 he was one of 21 Black men convicted of operating an 'illegal transportation system' — the boycott car pool — each given a 60-day suspended sentence and a $500 fine, with the convictions on appeal.
charges: Operating an unlicensed transportation system — the Tallahassee boycott car pool

name: Dan B. Speed
bio: Dan B. Speed was the car-pool coordinator of the Inter-Civic Council in Tallahassee, arrested without warrant and convicted with Rev. C. K. Steele and 19 others in 1956 for operating the bus-boycott car pool as an 'illegal transportation system.'
charges: Operating an unlicensed transportation system — the Tallahassee boycott car pool

name: Wilhelmina Jakes
bio: Wilhelmina Jakes was a Florida A&M College student arrested with Carrie Patterson on May 26, 1956 — on a charge of 'placing themselves in a position to incite a riot' — for taking the only open bus seats, beside a white woman. Their arrest touched off the Tallahassee bus boycott.
charges: 'Placing oneself in a position to incite a riot' — for defying bus segregation

name: Carrie Patterson
bio: Carrie Patterson was a Florida A&M College student arrested with Wilhelmina Jakes on May 26, 1956 for sitting in the only available bus seats, next to a white woman — the incident that launched the Tallahassee bus boycott.
charges: 'Placing oneself in a position to incite a riot' — for defying bus segregation
